questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Ever since meeting my current roommate (who's Canadian) here in Copenhagen, I was SO inspired to explore the country. Have always been a believer that if you're so lucky and privileged to get the chance to go abroad, go as far away as possible if you can! Of course Europe is lovely and has a LOT to offer, but personally I'm so, so happy I chose to visit a country further away and less generally accessible. When do I ever get the chance to randomly go to Canada again for 5 months?

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Western will send you so many mails with information, it's almost overwhelming. Especially if you're also in residence on campus (then double the amount of mails). Make sure to read the emails regularly to keep up with them! They are super good at providing information though, and Nicky Cottee is so sweet.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a ton of help to get, especially in the beginning. You always have someone to reach out to, and there's different orientation events for only exchange students in the beginning. They're really taking care of you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It was a little bit confusing understanding what on-campus residence were actually offered to exchange students, and it did also seem a bit random after being allocated to one. I was in Alumni House (all exchange students), and another exchange student from KU (same progamme) was in London Hall with the (younger) second years students. It seemed that neither of these two residences had a great community, maybe London Hall but more so for the actual full time students at Western. It is also possible to rent an apartment on campus too, and to my understanding, Western will basically just act as the landlord and not get involved more than that. In Alumni House you live 4 students with a shared bathroom, kitchen, and living room.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Meal plans were available for the exchange students in Alumni House for a pretty expensive price. The canteen was located in a building a short walk from Alumni House. The apartment at Alumni House had a kitchen, but NO kitchen appliances what so ever (only oven, fridge etc.). You have to buy everything (I can highly recommend Goodwill for this!) or maybe ask in Facebook-groups if anyone wants to sell, let you use or even donate some kitchen appliances. I personally am very happy I didn't have a meal plan - instead I explored the dining options around the city, campus, cooked at home and was invited over by new (local) friends!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
As an exchange student, you could apply for housing on campus. But beware! It's sort of a first come first serve concept after the application platform opens, so apply early. The vibes at Alumni House were not very good - not really a community per say, which was very surprising since we were all exchange students! I personally just think when there's no real initiative, like any traditions or events, planned by the university, it's difficult to start this sense of community. BUT you will live with 3 other students, and you might be lucky that they match your personality well. Also, apparently around homecoming (especially) and halloween, there's rules to how many friends you can gather in the apartment because of the huge amount of noise, people and partying going on. Western Housing will inform you about this.

Final thoughs: It's quite expensive to live on-campus, and I'm not sure it's worth the money, because of the lack of community in Alumni House. This only specifically applies to Alumni House (I think), because all other residences is for first year students (and a few for second year students), and there's a whole thing going on with activities and "res"-lifestyle for the first years (they're around 19 y/o). NOT the same thing with exchange students, lol! Also, campus is quite far from downtown, and this is where the fun happens if you're somewhat a party person. Therefore, if I could do my exchange semester over, I would definitely consider finding a great place off campus (downtown!).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was quite different than the registration process at KU. Here, it's a bidding system, so you'll get a certain amount of points you can spread out as you wish over X amount of courses you want. You will also get access to statistics on how many points you needed to offer for this course last year - it's kind of a supply and demand system: If the course has few spots and lots of students are interested, it'll cost more points in order to increase your chances to get into the course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always reach out to Nicky Cottee, she replies fast!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all the classes that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I can really recommend taking a look at the stats to get a feeling of how to distribute your points. There might be a course you expect to be super popular, but then you'll see that almost everybody gets into the course + the opposite! Also, you'll only get access to the actual course catalogue a month or so before the semester starts, and you'll realize that half the courses you wanted is in the spring semester / fall semester! But there were still lots of cool courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: To my knowledge, everybody in law school at Western (maybe this applies to Ontario or even Canada), has a bachelors degree (undergrad) in *something*, could literally be whatever. Met a girl who did her undergrad in biology, and another one in literature or something. So law school at Western is really only 3 years TOTAL, where our in Denmark i 3 + 2 years. The level of courses was not the same in all courses, and this highly depended on the professor. One of my courses was almost too easy and another one was really challenging for me.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It *really* depends on your prof. I had a total of four courses, and in one of them, the prof would randomly call out students to answer questions, in the second one the prof was just monologuing for 90 minutes straight, in the third one every student participated so much it made you feel bad to not say anything in class. Also, attendance is mandatory, which honestly is great (and something I think KU should do more), because it creates a great sense of community in the classroom - you know that you'll see your classmates. I'd say participation is expected on paper, but not all professors cares about it equally. EXAMS: In neither of my courses, I had to attend a physical sit-down-for-5-hours-exam or oral exam - all of my courses would end with a written paper at around 12-25 pages per course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Environmental Law
Food Law
Outer Space Law
Intellectual Property Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was happy with all of my courses. The prof in Environmental Law was super down to earth (easiest course of the four). Food Law was quite challenging, because the prof really expected a lot of the students individually. We did two simulations / negotiations during the semester, and this was being taken very seriously, and generally there was a huge focus on discussions in the classroom. Outer Space Law was super cool too, and the prof is super sweet and helpful. Intellectual Property Law is also a great course, the classes are more like lectures, where there's less student participation (than say, Food Law).

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Since the transit system in London Ontario is so bad and unpredictable (at least it was included in your Western One Card!), I ended up Uber'ing a LOT. This was not always absolutely necessary, but sometimes the busses were so inconvenient, that I saw Uber'ing places as an investment in utilising my limited time in Canada, lol! It can also be rather cheap sometimes.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: VIA RAIL... The only (basically) train system in Canada is ridiculously expensive - it can be cheaper flying. I can recommend renting a car, it's much cheaper than you'd expect (book a giant pick up truck just because you can).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a club for pretty much anything you can imagine, and the students really cares about it! It's SOOO great, and I really wish it was like that at KU. Western will host some sort of club-day in september where you can walk around to all the clubs (i think there's more than 150) and chat with them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Travel! Join clubs! And if you go to bars and social events arranged by the university, chat with the locals!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go travel as much as you can! London can be quite boring. It's so easy to catch a flixbus to Toronto or even go to The States. Montreal is cool (Quebec is very different from the rest of Canada) and Calgary / Banff was a blast!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy! Took me some time to understand the tipping culture though! Ask a local about this.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to all the social events arranged by the university, get to know your roommates, and enjoy the openness and friendliness of Canadian people!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The tipping and in general dining / service culture! If you're at a bar and you sit by the table, you have a server, and you're not supposed to go up to the bar and order. Also, it's mandatory for bars / pubs to serve food (at least in Ontario), and the food is usually totally allright!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness of Canadians. They are really including you in whatever. I was invited over for Thanksgiving by three different people / families and spent Christmas there as well!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Your performance in class and grade is not everything - you're on exchange! View it as one big learning experience in so many other ways than just academically. 
2) You will be invited to stuff. Say YES to everything (if you're comfortable), even if someone is just inviting you to go grocery shopping. 
3) I went to Canada in the end of July 2025 and got home at the end of January 2026 - best decision ever. Added two whole months to the exchange semester! Do the same if you can!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring your physical driver's licence, because you WILL be ID'd, even at restaurants.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Canadian people are truly amazing. They will make you feel at home SO quickly. They love small talk - enjoy it!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Whenever the time came to write the final papers, it was tough at times. But a great alternative to the classic 5 hour exam in law school in DK. 
2) Returning home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go! Go! Go!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
